Title: Toward Open-Source Chiplets for HPC and AI: Occamy and Beyond
Text:
Toward Open-Source Chiplets for HPC and AI:
Occamy and Beyond
Paul Scheffler*, Thomas Benz*, Tim Fischer*, Lorenzo Leone*, Sina Arjmandpour*, Luca Benini*†
* Integrated Systems Laboratory, ETH Zurich, Switzerland
† Department of Electrical, Electronic, and Information Engineering, University of Bologna, Italy
{paulsc,tbenz,fischeti,lleone,sarjmandpour,lbenini}@iis.ee.ethz.ch
Abstract—We present a roadmap for open-source chiplet-based RISC-
V systems targeting high-performance computing and artificial intel-
ligence, aiming to close the performance gap to proprietary designs.
Starting with Occamy, the first open, silicon-proven dual-chiplet RISC-V
manycore in 12nm FinFET, we scale to Ramora, a mesh-NoC-based dual-
chiplet system, and to Ogopogo, a 7nm quad-chiplet concept architecture
achieving state-of-the-art compute density. Finally, we explore possible
avenues to extend openness beyond logic-core RTL into simulation, EDA,
PDKs, and off-die PHYs.
Index Terms—Chiplets, RISC-V, HPC, NoC, AI, Machine Learning
I. INTRODUCTION
Soaring compute demands and rapidly growing datasets in arti-
ficial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) are
outpacing the performance and memory bandwidth advances offered
by technology scaling. As the gap widens with the slowdown of tech-
nology scaling, system designers are turning to increasingly large and
specialized architectures to sustain performance and energy efficiency
needs. However, single-die packaging has emerged as a bottleneck,
constraining designs in terms of area, yield, and connectivity [1].
These limitations are driving a transition toward 2.5D integration,
wherein multiple discrete chiplets are interconnected at short distance
and fine pitch through an interposer. The yield, scale, and die-to-die
bandwidth of 2.5D systems vastly exceed those of single-die packages,
unlocking further scaling. Standardized interfaces and ecosystems, as
proposed by the Open Chiplet Architecture [2], would allow chiplets to
serve as interchangeable building blocks, enabling further architectural
specialization and sustained performance and efficiency gains.
The idea of an open, composable chiplet ecosystem naturally
aligns with the goals and principles of open-source hardware, which
has made significant progress in recent years [3]. Like open-source
IPs, open-source chiplets could become important building blocks in
future 2.5D systems, providing many of the same benefits including
high design transparency, low integration cost, and low barriers to
design collaboration [1]. The main drawback of current open-source
designs is their limited performance: as shown in Fig. 1, there is a
significant performance gap between state-of-the-art (SoA) and open-
source systems demonstrated in silicon, which grows larger as the
degree of openness increases. For instance, systems designed with
open electronic design automation (EDA) like SeyrITA [4] feature at
most a few processing elements, while Basilisk [3], an end-to-end
open-source design using an open process design kit (PDK), features
only a single core. To enable the proliferation of open-source chiplets
and their benefits, designers must close this performance gap by
working toward open chiplet designs with competitive performance.
In this paper, we present our evolving roadmap on open-source 2.5D

We begin with Occamy [5], our first chiplet-based system and the
first open-source 2.5D RISC-V manycore demonstrated in silicon. Oc-
camy’s 432 compute cores feature multiple instruction set architecture
(ISA) extensions to efficiently handle the mixed-regularity compute
of modern HPC and AI workloads, achieving a peak performance
of 876 DP-GFLOP/s as well as competitive (89%) and leading (42–
83%) peak FPU utilizations on regular (dense) and irregular (sparse)
workloads, respectively. While Occamy’s compute architecture proved
highly effective, we found that its interconnect, based on centralized
crossbars, limits the scalability of its architecture to larger systems.
To address this, we propose Ramora [6], our second-generation
dual-chiplet system featuring a scalable, low-overhead 2D mesh
network-on-chip (NoC). Ramora extends Occamy’s clusters with co-
integrated NoC routers to enable their 2D tiling, significantly reducing
interconnect overheads. This enables 33% more clusters and an 11%
higher peak clock on the same chiplet area, raising compute density
by 43% and increasing peak performance to 1.29 DP-TFLOP/s. It also
provides enough bandwidth at its mesh edge for a 16× faster 1.04 Tb/s
die-to-die (D2D) interface. Despite these benefits, we identify further
opportunities to improve on Ramora’s architecture by expanding the
compute mesh and accelerating data movement in the NoC.
These insights lead us to Ogopogo, a concept architecture ex-
panding Ramora’s compute mesh to a quad-chiplet, quad-HBM3,
10.3 DP-TFLOP/s system in 7 nm FinFET. In addition to its 8.0×
higher peak performance and 2.8× higher compute density, Ogo-
pogo introduces three lightweight extensions accelerating common
NoC communication patterns: packed irregular streams, in-stream
DMA operations, and in-router collectives. With Ogopogo’s node-
normalized compute density exceeding that of Nvidia’s SoA B200

our 2.5D designs: in addition to the open register transfer level (RTL)

To summarize, our contributions are as follows:
• We review and discuss Occamy (Section II), our silicon-proven
dual-chiplet, dual-HBM2E, 876 DP-GFLOP/s RISC-V manycore
in 12 nm FinFET designed to efficiently handle both dense and
sparse HPC and AI workloads. We discuss Occamy’s main lim-
itation, namely its interconnect based on hierarchical crossbars,
which limits its efficiency and scalability to larger systems.
• We present Ramora (Section III), our second-generation dual-
chiplet system tiling Occamy’s proven clusters in a scalable, low-
overhead 2D mesh NoC. On the same chiplet area, Ramora pro-
vides 33% more clusters and a 16× faster D2D link, reaching
up to 1.29 DP-TFLOP/s. While Ramora is highly area-efficient,
we identify further opportunities in expanding its compute mesh
and accelerating inefficient data movement in its NoC.
• We propose Ogopogo (Section IV), a 7 nm quad-chiplet, quad-
HBM3 concept architecture scaling up Ramora’s compute mesh
to 10.3 DP-TFLOP/s while introducing three lightweight data
movement extensions: in-router collectives, in-stream DMA oper-
ations, and packed irregular streams. Ogopogo’s node-normalized
compute density exceeds that of Nvidia’s B200 GPU by 19%.
• We explore how to expand the openness of future chiplet-based
architectures (Section V). In addition to open-RTL logic cores,
we explore the possibilities of open simulation, open EDA, and
even open PDKs and off-die PHYs.
II. OCCAMY: A DUAL-CHIPLET SILICON DEMONSTRATOR
Occamy [5] is our first chiplet-based system and the first open-
source 2.5D RISC-V manycore demonstrated in silicon. It features
two 12 nm FinFET compute chiplets on a passive 65 nm interposer,
each paired with 16 GiB of HBM2E DRAM and connected through a
fully digital D2D link. Its 432 RV32G compute cores feature multiple
ISA extensions [7]–[10] to efficiently handle the sparse and mixed-
precision compute of modern HPC and AI applications, achieving
competitive (89%) and leading (42–83%) peak FPU utilizations on
dense and sparse workloads, respectively. The cores are organized
into 48 clusters, which communicate through a hierarchical crossbar
interconnect and leverage explicit, DMA-based data movement.
Section II-A presents Occamy’s hierarchical architecture. In Sec-
tion II-B, we shortly discuss Occamy’s silicon implementation. Sec-
tion II-C presents our silicon evaluation, focusing on the compute
utilization and energy efficiency benefits of Occamy’s ISA extensions
and cluster architecture. Finally, Section II-D will compare Occamy
to existing CPUs, GPUs, and accelerators, and discuss the scalability
challenges arising from its hierarchical crossbar interconnect.
A. Architecture

shows Occamy’s compute cluster, which is based on [7]. Each cluster
comprises eight worker cores and a DMA control core, which share
a 32-bank, 128 KiB scratchpad memory (SPM) and an 8 KiB L1
instruction cache. Each worker core, shown in Fig. 2a, features a 64-

Two worker-core ISA extensions maximize FPU utilization on both
regular and irregular workloads: a floating-point hardware loop [7] and
three sparsity-capable streaming units (SUs) [8]. All three SUs support
up to 4D strided accesses to the shared SPM to accelerate regular
workloads. Two SUs additionally support indirect streams with 8-to-
32-bit indices to accelerate scatter-gather accesses in SPM. Finally,
both indirect SUs can cooperate to accelerate sparse tensor intersection
and union, with the third SU optionally writing out the joint indices
for sparse result tensors. Together, each core’s SUs enable a sustained
bandwidth into the shared SPM of up to 24 B per cycle.
The DMA control core features a tightly-coupled 512-bit DMA en-
gine [10], which enables high-bandwidth. asynchronous ≤2D transfers
between external memory and the cluster SPM. This core coordinates
the computation of worker cores and their fine-grained, low-latency
accesses to the SPM with the latency-tolerant DMA transfers of large,
double-buffered data tiles. To reduce backpressure in the chiplet-level
interconnect, the DMA engine has priority access to the shared SPM
through a secondary interconnect; it accesses contiguous blocks of
eight banks at once, transferring up to 64 B per cycle.
Fig. 2c shows Occamy’s chiplet-level architecture, which comprises
a compute and a host domain. The compute domain is hierarchically
organized into six groups of four clusters each. Grouped clusters have
full-bandwidth access to each other through two AXI4 crossbars: a
512-bit crossbar used by DMA engines and instruction caches, and an
atomics-capable 64-bit crossbar used for synchronization and message
passing. Each group shares one outgoing and one incoming port per
crossbar to the chiplet-level interconnect, providing 64 GiB/s for bulk
transfers and 8 GiB/s for message passing. The outgoing 512-bit port
additionally features a shared, configurable 32 KiB constant cache.

At the chiplet level, the 512-bit ports of all six groups connect to
an intra-group crossbar, interconnecting the groups, and to an HBM
crossbar connecting to all eight HBM2E controllers. A 512-bit system
crossbar bridges the 64-bit and 512-bit networks and provides access
to a chiplet-level DMA engine, 1 MiB of SPM for fast chiplet-level
communication, as well as a 512-bit D2D port. All 64-bit group ports
connect to the 64-bit SoC crossbar, which also connects the host
domain and a 64-bit D2D port. The host domain is built around a
Linux-capable RV64GC CVA6 core [11], which is used to dispatch
and orchestrate on-chiplet computation; it provides various peripherals
and a dedicated 512 KiB SPM for host management tasks.
The D2D link features two segments connecting to the two on-
chip networks: a narrow (64-bit) segment with a single PHY and
a wide (512-bit) segment with 38 PHYs. Both segments serialize
their networks’ AXI4 transactions to AXI-Stream for transmission.
Each PHY features an all-digital, source-synchronous duplex inter-
face with eight double-data-rate (DDR) lanes in each direction. The
transmitter side forwards a divided system clock, while the receiver
side synchronizes packets to its system clock to reassemble them. The
wide segment features a channel allocator to enable fault tolerance:
an initial calibration detects faulty PHYs, which can individually be
disabled. The narrow and wide segments achieve effective duplex
bandwidths of up to 1.33 Gb/s and 64 Gb/s, respectively.
B. Implementation
The full 2.5D Occamy system was implemented and fabricated
along with a carrier board, resulting in the compute module shown
in Figure 3b. The two compute dies with their respective Micron
MT54A16G808A00AC-32 HBM2E stacks were mounted on Hedwig, a
passive, four-layer 65 nm PKG-25SI interposer from GlobalFoundries.
The compute chiplets were implemented in GlobalFoundries’ 12 nm
LP+ FinFET technology using Synopsys Fusion Compiler. We used
7.5-track standard cells from Arm and HBM2E IPs (controller and
PHY) provided by Rambus. We targeted a nominal compute clock
of 1 GHz, achieving up to 1.14 GHz under typical conditions (0.8 V,
25 °C), and 0.95 GHz under worst-case conditions (0.72 V, 125 °C).
Figs. 3a and 3b show the annotated physical layouts of the com-
pute cluster and chiplet, respectively. The 1.0 mm2 cluster is area-
dominated by its nine compute cores (44%) and SPM (17%). Each
group (Gn) is dominated by its clusters (83%). The top-level chiplet
layout is dominated by its compute groups (39%), HBM2E interface
(25%), and D2D link (11%). The west and south chiplet edges are
reserved for the HBM2E and D2D interfaces, respectively, while off-
interposer IO drivers are kept on the north and west edges.
C. Evaluation
We evaluated Occamy’s performance, power consumption, and
energy efficiency on various dense, sparse, and mixed-regularity
workloads with and without SU acceleration. We provided its nominal
1 GHz clock and typical operating conditions (25 °C, 0.8 V).
Figure 4a presents our results on increasingly irregular double-
buffered FP64 workloads. Occamy’s SUs accelerate dense general
matrix multiply (GEMM) by 2.7×, reaching a near-ideal FPU utiliza-
tion of 89%, a performance of 686 GFLOP/s, and an energy efficiency
of 39.8 GFLOP/s/W. Stencil computations (STC) are accelerated by
up to 3.9×, reaching up to 83% FPU utilization, 571 GFLOP/s, and
28.1 GFLOP/s/W. On graph convolutional network (GCN) layers, Oc-
camy’s SUs provide speedups of up to 2.3× and reach up to 54% FPU
utilization, 413 GFLOP/s, and 25.0 GFLOP/s/W. Finally, SUs accel-
erate sparse-dense matrix multiply (SpMM) by up to 4.6×, achieving
up to 42% FPU utilization, 307 GFLOP/s, and 16.0 GFLOP/s/W.
Figure 4b shows Occamy’s performance and energy efficiency on
SU-accelerated GEMM with decreasing precision. We consider FP16
GEMM with and without expanding FP32 accumulation (EXP suffix)
and FP8 GEMM only with expanding FP16 accumulation. As we
reduce precision, the performance and energy efficiency scale as ex-
pected, incurring slight conversion and packing overheads. On expand-
ing FP8 GEMM, Occamy achieves a throughput of 4.1 QP-TFLOP/s
and an energy efficiency of 263 QP-GFLOP/s/W. On FP16, expanding
GEMM is 6.5% more energy-efficient than non-expanding GEMM
thanks to dedicated expanding dot product units in our FPU [9].
Figure 4c presents Occamy’s performance and energy efficiency on
SU-accelerated FP16 GPT-J inference in non-autoregressive mode. We
leverage the implementation presented in [12], using FlashAttention-
2 for the attention mechanism. At the shortest considered sequence
length of 128, Occamy achieves a peak throughput of 490 tok/s and
an energy efficiency of 29.3 tok/s/W. Increasing the sequence length
gradually decreases throughput due to the quadratic scaling of the
attention computation. Accordingly, we also see a gradual decrease in
energy efficiency, as less time is spent on matrix multiplication and
more time on the less efficient element-wise softmax operation.
Finally, we evaluate the utilization, energy efficiency, and latency
of our fully digital D2D link. On a 16 KiB transfer, the 64 Gb/s wide
segment achieves a link utilization of 96% and an energy efficiency
of 1.6 pJ/b. Using the host core to access the other chiplet’s host SPM
through the narrow segment incurs 27 cycles of latency, while a DMA
transfer over the wide segment exhibits 61 cycles of latency.
D. SoA Comparison and Discussion
We extensively compared Occamy to SoA CPUs, GPUs, and
accelerators [5]. Unlike domain-specific accelerators targeting sparse

compute, Occamy is a general-purpose system that efficiently handles
both one- and two-sided sparse operations across a wide sparsity range
and with high dataflow flexibility. Its peak performance far exceeds
most academic RISC-V prototypes and is comparable to commercial
products like Sophon’s SG2042 [13]. On dense workloads, its 89%
FPU utilization is competitive with SoA CPUs and GPUs, and its
energy efficiency roughly matches that of Nvidia’s A100 [14]. On
stencil codes, Occamy’s SUs enable a leading FPU utilization and
node-normalized area efficiency, outperforming A100 by 1.7× [15]
and 1.2× [16], respectively. On sparse-dense linear algebra, Occamy
further expands its lead on SoA CPUs and GPUs, achieving a
5.2× [17] higher FPU utilization and an 11× [18] higher node-
normalized area efficiency than leading competitors. To summarize,
Occamy’s FPU utilization and efficiency are competitive on regular
workloads while leading the SoA on irregular workloads.
While Occamy’s cluster-based compute architecture is highly effec-
tive across various workloads, its hierarchical crossbar-based intercon-
nect poses significant scalability challenges for future systems. Despite
our careful hierarchical design, 31% of the compute domain’s area is
dedicated to crossbars, leaving only 65% to the compute clusters. As
we scale up Occamy’s architecture, several fundamental limitations of
this interconnect emerge. First, crossbar area scales with the product of
requestor and endpoint counts, progressively reducing the area fraction
available for compute. Second, the centralized architecture of cross-
bars leads to longer global routes and higher routing congestion, even-
tually degrading the quality of results (QoR) despite parameter tuning
and numerous routing iterations. Finally, crossbar-based interconnects
limit off-die bandwidth, as routing traffic from any requestor to any
off-die channel requires increasingly large crossbars. In fact, Occamy’s
HBM crossbar required careful design and tuning to maintain both
physical implementability and full HBM bandwidth. While this was
manageable with Occamy’s low-throughput, fully digital D2D link,
adopting an SoA high-bandwidth D2D interface alongside HBM2E
would have significantly complicated implementation.
To overcome these overheads and scalability limitations, a common
solution is to adopt a mesh-based NoC [6], [19], [20]. Unlike crossbars
that funnel traffic through a few congested nodes, a NoC distributes
communication across routers and links that scale linearly, rather than
quadratically, with system size. By integrating routers into compute
tiles, connections can be formed through abutment, simplifying imple-
mentation. In the next section, we therefore present an Occamy-scale
system that tiles its clusters into a scalable mesh NoC to overcome
the design, area, and implementation challenges we identified above.
III. RAMORA: A SCALABLE CROSS-CHIPLET MESH
Ramora [6] is our second-generation open-source 2.5D system. It
maintains Occamy’s highly effective cluster architecture, but adopts
a 2D mesh NoC to reduce interconnect area overheads and improve
system scalability. Compared to Occamy, Ramora features 33% more
clusters on the same chiplet area and reaches an 11% higher clock
speed, achieving a 43% higher compute density and a peak perfor-
mance of 1.29 TFLOP/s. Its 0.15 pJ/B/hop NoC increases HBM2E
bandwidth utilization in low- and high-traffic scenarios by 11% and
22%, respectively, and can accommodate an improved four-port D2D
link architecture with a 16× higher wide-data bandwidth of 1.04 Tb/s.
In Section III-A, we present Ramora’s architectural innovations
over Occamy, focusing on its mesh NoC and improved D2D link.
Section III-B discusses the implementation of Ramora’s compute
domain and a possible chiplet implementation. Section III-C presents
our evaluation, focusing on the bandwidth, latency, and performance
improvements enabled by Ramora’s NoC. Finally, Section III-D will
compare Ramora to existing mesh NoC systems and discuss possible
next steps to scale up and improve our chiplet architecture.
A. Architecture
Ramora uses FlooNoC [6] as its top-level interconnect, a wide-link
mesh NoC serializing both narrow (64-bit) and wide (512-bit) AXI4
transactions. Each link consists of three statically routed physical
channels: the unidirectional req and rsp channels transport requests
and 64-bit data, while the bidirectional wide channel transports 512-bit
bulk data. FlooNoC provides two network interface (NI) variants, one
with a reorder buffer (ROB) and one without. The ROB-less NI stalls
outgoing requests whenever necessary to enforce ordering, requiring
an out-of-order-capable requestor to maintain high throughput.
Ramora largely reuses Occamy’s cluster design, but extends it with
an integrated NI and router so it can be tiled into a mesh. The
resulting architecture is shown in Fig. 5a. The cluster’s NI is ROB-
less: instead of incurring a large ROB, the DMA engine is extended to
distribute transfers onto multiple backends [10], enabling out-of-order
processing. The cluster router fully interconnects five ports, one for
each cardinal direction and one for the local NI. It supports multiple
static routing algorithms (source-based, dimension-ordered, or table-
based) as well as wormhole routing to prevent write burst interleaving.
Instead of leveraging virtual channels, each of the three physical
channels is routed independently, ensuring network-level isolation.

virtual 16×4 mesh that spans across both chiplets. In total, Ramora’s
D2D link provides an effective duplex bandwidth of 1.04 Tb/s for wide
transfers and 137 Gb/s for narrow transfers.

C. Evaluation
We evaluate Ramora’s on-chip latency, HBM bandwidth utilization,
and peak performance and compare them to those of Occamy. We
focus on evaluating the benefits of Ramora’s NoC, as both systems
share the same compute cluster architecture.
Fig. 7a compares the average, minimum, and maximum inter-cluster
latency under zero and full interconnect load. Overall, Ramora’s
NoC trades a modest latency increase for a significantly improved
scalability, as many lightweight routers and links replace a few huge
crossbars. Minimum latencies are higher on Ramora due to Occamy’s
dedicated inter-group links, whereas maximum latencies are higher
due to the linear increase of hop counts in 2D meshes. Average
latencies, however, are very similar in both systems, being 0.4%
smaller in Ramora under zero load and only 8.4% higher under full
load. Thus, Ramora manages to combine the low average latencies of

Fig. 7b compares the single-channel HBM2E bandwidth utilization
of one cluster’s DMA engine under zero and full HBM load from
other clusters. The peak achievable full-load utilization is 25%, as
four clusters each share the bandwidth of one 512-bit link. Under
zero load, Ramora notably increases the average bandwidth utilization
from 84.7% to 96.6%, thanks to fewer hops and routing steps to the
memory controllers. Under full load, Ramora’s advantage becomes
even more pronounced, increasing average utilization from 20.2%
to 24.8%. This is because HBM channels are no longer accessed
through a single crossbar, but distributed among edge routers, reducing
contention. Overall, Ramora’s decentralized mesh routing enables
significant HBM bandwidth utilization benefits.
Fig. 7c compares the peak FP64 performance of Ramora and
Occamy, both at 1 GHz and at their respective 1.26 GHz and 1.14 GHz
peak clocks under typical conditions. At 1 GHz, Ramora’s additional
clusters increase peak performance from 768 to 1024 GFLOP/s. At
peak clock, Ramora’s further expands its lead thanks to its 11% higher
clock speed, increasing peak performance from 876 to 1290 GFLOP/s.
Thus, Ramora significantly improves on Occamy’s peak performance
by increasing both its cluster count and its peak clock speed.
Finally, we assess the energy efficiency of Ramora’s NoC. We esti-
mate the power consumption of an otherwise idle cluster performing
a 4 KiB DMA transfer to a neighboring tile in post-layout simulation.
Of the cluster tile’s 128 mW draw, only 15% were consumed by the
components actively involved in the transfer. The routers themselves
consumed only 596 pJ, yielding an energy efficiency of 0.15 pJ/B/hop.
D. SoA Comparison and Discussion
We compared Ramora to SoA 2D mesh NoC systems [6] including
Piton [19], Celerity [21], and ESP [20]. Among all considered
systems, Ramora achieves the highest simplex tile-to-tile bandwidth
and energy efficiency, 2.6× and 3.0× higher than the runner-ups
ESP and Celerity, respectively. At the same time, the NoC’s power
contribution in Ramora is 4.0× lower than in ESP. Ramora has the
second-lowest NoC area overhead after Piton, which provides much
lower bandwidths and narrower links. Only ESP was evaluated in an
equally advanced technology (also 12 nm FinFET), while only Celerity
can exceed Ramora’s peak clock speed. While Celerity’s larger 8×62
mesh naturally provides a larger aggregate NoC bandwidth, Ramora
features the largest total link data width. Overall, while Ramora does
not feature the largest 2D mesh NoC yet, its wide, low-overhead links
enable leading tile-to-tile bandwidth and energy efficiency.
With Ramora, we combined Occamy’s proven compute cluster ar-
chitecture with a scalable, low-overhead 2D mesh NoC providing lead-
ing throughput and efficiency. However, there are still opportunities
to improve our open-source chiplet-based designs. First and foremost,
Ramora’s highly scalable NoC allows for even larger meshes: by
increasing the chiplet size and moving to a more advanced technology
node, we could further expand the compute domain. This would
also provide more edge links, enabling even higher HBM and D2D
bandwidths; we could even leverage the remaining free mesh edge
to add a second D2D link, enabling quad-chiplet systems. Secondly,
we could extend the clusters, routers, and endpoints with specialized
hardware units to reduce NoC communication overheads. By reducing
redundant and inefficient NoC traffic, we can reduce the energy cost
of both on- and off-chip data movement and accelerate memory-bound
workloads, improving both performance and energy efficiency.
Based on these insights, the next section will present the con-
cept architecture of our next open-source 2.5D design, which scales
Ramora’s architecture to four larger chiplets while introducing three
new extensions accelerating common NoC communication patterns.
IV. OGOPOGO: A QUAD-CHIPLET CONCEPT ARCHITECTURE
Ogopogo is a quad-chiplet 7 nm concept architecture that scales
up Ramora’s compute mesh to an 8× higher peak performance. It
introduces three lightweight extensions improving data movement ef-
ficiency: in-router collectives, in-stream DMA operations, and packed
irregular streams. To sustain the higher edge bandwidth of its larger
chiplet mesh, Ogopogo upgrades from HBM2E to HBM3, doubling
the per-chiplet bandwidth. An estimated implementation of Ogopogo
achieves a peak performance of 10.3 DP-TFLOP/s and a peak compute
density of 41.1 DP-GFLOP/s/mm2, 19% higher than that achieved by
Nvidia’s B200 GPU [22] when normalized to our 7 nm target node.
In Section IV-A, we will describe Ogopogo’s quad-chiplet archi-
tectures and its data movement extensions. In Section IV-B, we will
evaluate a possible implementation of Ogopogo and compare the full
evolution of our 2.5D manycore designs to Nvidia’s SoA B200 GPU.
In the following Section V, we will explore avenues to expand the
openness of our 2.5D systems beyond logic-core RTL descriptions.
A. Architecture
Figure 8 shows Ogopogo’s concept architecture. Each of the four
7 nm chiplets features a 16×8 compute mesh, reusing Ramora’s scal-
able NoC architecture and introducing the data movement extensions
we describe below. The left mesh edge now provides a 6.4 Gb/s/pin
HBM3 interface, whose increased bandwidth and parallelism can serve
requests from all 16 edge routers. The bottom and right mesh edges
feature D2D links reusing Ramora’s LVDS PHYs, which provide
wide-transfer bandwidths of 1.02 Tb/s and 2.05 Tb/s to the respective
neighboring chiplets. The top mesh edge now connects the remaining
chiplet resources including the host domain, system DMA, system
SPM, and off-interposer IO. We update the host domain to our
standardized Cheshire platform [23], which supports multi-core hosts,
multi-port NoC connections, and additional peripherals.
Ogopogo’s DMA engines, routers, and HBM3 endpoints feature
three lightweight hardware extensions which improve NoC bandwidth
efficiency and accelerate common communication patterns:
In-router collectives: We extend the routers with fork and join
primitives to handle collective communication patterns like multicast,
broadcast, and barriers inside the NoC rather than at the endpoints.

barrier synchronization, we instead join the inflight requests from
multiple sources and then fork the response back to all sources. These
capabilities come at a modest cost, increasing router area by less than
10% without degrading system timing.
In-stream operations: We extend the cluster DMA engines with
in-stream vector units, which can perform simple element-wise and
reductive operations on the fly. Once read in by the engine, the data
stream is aligned to its element boundary and passed through a multi-
function compute unit. Element-wise operations include addition and
multiplication with a constant, allowing for the scaling or normal-
ization of vectors. Reduction operations include both arithmetic and
logical reductions. An in-stream unit operating on 64-bit integers in-
creases DMA engine area by only 80 kGE while accelerating element-
wise scaling by up to 32× and arithmetic reductions by up to 12×.
Packed irregular streams: We extend the cluster DMA engines
and HBM3 endpoints with irregular stream packing and unpacking
support. This enables strided and indexed access streams to pack
tightly into wide NoC flits, significantly improving link utilization and
effective throughput on irregular workloads involving narrow HBM
accesses. The cluster-side extension provides scatter-gather DMA
jobs, using index arrays in the cluster SPM. These jobs generate
parallel streams of narrow (≤64-bit) requests, up to eight of which are
packed into one wide flit. The HBM-side extension then unpacks these
requests and combines them into minimum-size (256-bit) accesses
using a temporal coalescer. A 161 kGE packing unit improves the
bandwidth efficiency of random-index scatter-gather by 4.8×, ideally
enabling up to 8× improvements depending on the access pattern.
B. Evaluation and SoA Comparison
We estimate the area and timing of Ogopogo’s compute chiplets in
TSMC’s 7 nm FinFET technology based on a full cluster implementa-
tion with Fusion Compiler, Ramora’s existing D2D PHY design, and
the HBM3E interfaces of Nvidia’s Blackwell (B200) GPU [22]. De-
spite their significant performance benefits presented in Section IV-A,
we find that the combined area impact of our data movement exten-
sions is only 5.3%. Overall, we estimate that Ogopogo’s chiplets are
each 112 mm2 in area and can operate at up to 1.26 GHz under typical
conditions; this yields a peak performance of 10.3 DP-TFLOP/s and
a peak compute density of 41.1 DP-GFLOP/s/mm2.

V. TOWARD END-TO-END OPEN-SOURCE CHIPLETS
So far, our chiplet-based designs have primarily offered synthe-
sizable, open-source RTL descriptions of their logic cores. However,
making the source of subsequent design stages freely available would
further enhance the benefits of our open-source hardware, promoting
greater design transparency, reducing integration costs, and lowering
barriers to collaboration between organizations. An end-to-end open-
source design, which can be reproduced without any proprietary tools
or IP, would even enable zero-trust, step-by-step verification by third
parties [3]. Therefore, in this section, we discuss different avenues to
further expand the openness of our 2.5D designs.
Simulation: Currently, our designs still rely on commercial
simulators for their robustness and feature completeness. Open-source
simulators like Verilator and Icarus Verilog exist, but are limited by
their scalability and lack of support for widespread SystemVerilog,
testbench, and gate-level constructs. However, they are rapidly im-
proving: basic RTL simulation of our logic core is already possible
in Verilator, with support for advanced verification features and gate-
level constructs like user-defined primitives (UDP) being under active
development. These improvements may soon enable full RTL and
gate-level simulation of our designs using open-source simulators.
EDA: Our implementations so far used commercial EDA tools,
which clearly outperform their open-source counterparts. However,
logic synthesis with Yosys and place-and-route with OpenROAD are
continuously improving their feature set and QoR, gradually closing


this gap [3]. We have already demonstrated our Cheshire host platform
in an end-to-end open-source 130 nm SoC [3] and are currently
implementing our cluster architecture in a 22 nm node using open
EDA tools [4]. Thus, implementing our full logic core in mature
technology nodes using only open EDA may soon be possible.
PDKs: Multiple open-source PDKs for manufacturable technolo-
gies, along with open cell libraries, have been released in recent
years. This includes GlobalFoundries’ 180 nm, SkyWater’s 130 nm,
and IHP’s 130 nm PDKs, as well as ICsprout’s recently released
55 nm PDK. We have already demonstrated our host subsystem in
IHP’s open technology [3]. However, these mature ≥55 nm nodes
are insufficient to produce high-complexity designs like our ≤12 nm
compute chiplets. This cannot be remedied by designers themselves,
but only by advanced foundries choosing to open-source their PDKs.
Off-die PHYs: High-speed PHYs for DRAM and D2D interfaces
may present the biggest hurdle to expanding openness, as their mixed-
signal nature requires expert design and is strongly coupled to the EDA
tools used and PDK targeted. Existing open-source SoCs often work
around this by falling back to slower, fully-digital interfaces [3], [23].
However, mixed-signal design for open PDKs is possible in principle,
as demonstrated by Efabless’ analog design flow [25]. Thus, open-
source PHYs could eventually become available, albeit subject to the
performance limitations of open-source EDA tools and PDKs.
In summary, as open-source simulation and EDA tools gradually
approach SoA quality, the lack of advanced open PDKs and the
inherent difficulty of open PHY design are emerging as the primary
challenges to further increasing the openness of our chiplet designs.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we presented our evolving roadmap for open-source,
chiplet-based RISC-V manycores targeting HPC and AI workloads
and aiming to close the performance gap to commercial silicon. We
began with Occamy, the first silicon-proven dual-chiplet, dual-HBM2E
RISC-V manycore in 12 nm FinFET, establishing an 876 DP-GFLOP/s
baseline with competitive (89%) and leading (42–83%) peak FPU
utilizations on regular and irregular workloads, respectively, and
thereby proving the efficacy of our cluster-based compute archi-
tecture. With Ramora, we then upgraded Occamy’s crossbar-based
interconnect to a scalable 0.15 pJ/B/hop 2D mesh NoC, raising peak
performance to 1.29 DP-TFLOP/s without increasing chiplet area and
improving compute density, high-load HBM bandwidth, and wide-
transfer D2D bandwidth by 43%, 22%, and 16×, respectively. Finally,
we proposed Ogopogo, a 7 nm quad-chiplet, quad-HBM3 concept
architecture scaling Ramora’s compute mesh to 10.3 DP-TFLOP/s and
introducing lightweight extensions for in-router collectives, in-stream
DMA operations, and packed irregular streams. Ogopogo exceeds
the node-normalized compute density of Nvidia’s SoA B200 GPU
by 19% while achieving a comparable energy efficiency and off-die
bandwidths, reducing the remaining performance gap to a matter of
die size. Our analysis demonstrates that open-source 2.5D designs can
scale to SoA performance in their digital core. If we raise our ambition
toward end-to-end open-source chiplets, we identify the lack of open
PDKs for advanced technologies and the challenges in open PHY
design as the main bottlenecks to be addressed in the future.

Abstract: We present a roadmap for open-source chiplet-based RISC- V systems targeting high-performance computing and artificial intel- ligence, aiming to close the performance gap to proprietary designs. Starting with Occamy, the first open, silicon-proven dual-chiplet RISC-V manycore in 12nm FinFET, we scale to Ramora, a mesh-NoC-based dual- chiplet system, and to Ogopogo, a 7nm quad-chiplet concept architecture achieving state-of-the-art compute density. Finally, we explore possible avenues to extend openness beyond logic-core RTL into simulation, EDA, PDKs, and off-die PHYs.
